speaker_role: independent counselor and instructor in a UCLA college counseling certificate program
commercial_incentive: Teaches a paid certificate course and points to her own course modules and YouTube tutorials.
key_insights: Define fit with four parts: academic, social, physical and financial, and weigh them equally.
Have students rank about ten priorities; the top three or four drive the search, since no college delivers everything.
Balance the list by acceptance-rate bands, keeping only a few very selective schools so students do not end up with all long shots.
When searching databases, start with broad filters and narrow gradually; too many required factors return zero results.
Structured research assignments (presentations to parents, reviewing majors, courses and clubs) increase student engagement.
Classify applications by workload, from transcript-only to full projects with essays and recommendations, so families plan effort.
Set internal deadlines well before real ones and plan for early rounds.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker's bands: 20% or lower acceptance = dream/wild card; 21-40% = reach; 40-60% = target; 60-100% = likely.
Recommended mix: 3-4 dream, 4-5 reach, 5-6 target, 3-4 likely; total 6 to 12, ideally about 10.
FAFSA allowed ten colleges at the time (speaker's statement); Common App limit of 20.
Speaker says colleges accept as much as 80 or 90 percent of their class in early rounds (unverified claim).
notable_or_distinctive: Provides an explicit acceptance-rate rubric and target counts per category, plus a four-legged-stool definition of fit.
reliability_notes: Rubric is one counselor's heuristic; some facts (FAFSA limit, US News lists from fall 2021, early-round percentage) are dated or unsupported.
